newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Central African Republic deal may avert bloodbath.
newsitem.headline: Central African Republic deal may avert bloodbath.

text.p: African mediators have offered the Central African Republic a ray of hope in the form of a peace deal to end its third army mutiny in under a year and halt a descent into ethnic bloodshed.

African peacekeepers are to replace troops from former colonial power France, who have been patrolling flashpoints in the riverside capital Bangui as a buffer between the mutineers and their foes in the loyalist presidential guard.
But a lasting solution is likely to depend on the commitment of politicians to true reconciliation and disarmament.
President Ange-Felix Patasse, his political rivals and Captain Anicet Saulet, leader of the mutineers, signed the Bangui Accords on Saturday in the impoverished country's national assembly building.
"National reconciliation is a vital commodity, a commodity without end," chief mediator General Amadou Toumani Toure, Mali's respected former military leader, told signatories.
"It's a permanent process to which we must commit ourselves, a flame which must be lit and jealously watched over."

The mediation launched by the presidents of Gabon, Mali, Chad and Burkina Faso in December at the behest of a Franco-African summit is the latest African attempt to find a home-grown solution to its many conflicts.
Pressure for Africa to put its own house in order increased after a U.N. bid to broker peace in Somalia, launched by U.S. troops amid much fanfare in 1992, turned sour.
In West Africa, Liberia's neighbours are trying to end seven years of civil war there and steer the shattered nation towards disarmament and elections in May.
Last year, Ivory Coast helped broker a peace deal in Sierra Leone. As with Liberia, that has yet to bring lasting peace.
The Central African Republic, a sprawling nation of just 3.5 million people, hit world headlines in the 1970s with the extravagant rule of self-proclaimed emperor Jean-Bedel Bokassa.

A French-backed coup toppled Bokassa in 1979 but after over a decade of military and single-party rule under Andre Kolingba, democratic change sweeping much of Africa after the collapse of Soviet communism hit Bangui.
Patasse, a northern civilian, won 1993 presidential elections -- with Kolingba trailing in fourth place.
Toumani Toure and the influential Roman Catholic Church say the mutinies have their roots in a wider social malaise.

They began in April and May over pay and conditions but turned into a campaign to oust Patasse. The latest revolt, which began on November 15, triggered ethnic killings. The mutineers, numbering about 700, are from Kolingba's minority Yakoma tribe.
The precise death toll is unclear. Some sources say it ran into hundreds, others say scores. Roman Catholic bishops, fearing another Rwanda, preached against ethnic hatred.
The peace blueprint envisages creation of a government of national unity, amnesties and restoration of constitutional legality within the democratic transition.
President Omar Bongo of Gabon told signatories democracy implied accepting political differences. "If we do not accept differences we have no democracy," he said.

Toumani Toure, launching round-table talks on January 11, told the rival groups they alone held the key to peace. "It is a challenge that demands commitment from the Central African Republic and its political class," he said.
All sides say proliferation of weapons is a major problem.

Patasse loyalists accused the mutineers of emptying the national armoury. The mutineers, whose stronghold is in the south of the capital close to the Oubangui River, accused Patasse of arming his own militia in other parts of the city.
"We hope the accords will bring disarmament and national reconciliation," Patasse spokesman Prospere Ndouba said.
"Peace will only come through the collection of weapons," Prime Minister Jean-Paul Ngoumpande told Reuters.
Bongo said that a 500-strong African peacekeeping force would deploy soon. It will include soldiers from Burkina Faso, Chad, Gabon, Mali, Senegal and Togo.
France, which has troops in the Central African Republic under a defence pact, lost two soldiers in the latest unrest.
French spokesman Colonel Henry Pelissier said French troops would provide logistical and technical support.
